nary_nodes.label: Friedman states Katharina Wagner changes remembrance culture
evidence: "I would like to state explicitly that Katharina Wagner is changing the culture of remembrance in Bayreuth." With these words, spoken from the stage of the Bayreuth Festival, German-Jewish author Michel Friedman encapsulated the central message of the festival's two-day opening celebration.

nary_nodes.label: Friedman's message on hatred and injustice
evidence: For the 70-year-old, whose family was almost entirely murdered during the Holocaust, the focus was on something more fundamental — the mechanisms that foster hatred and injustice, and the passivity of society that allows them to flourish. His message was about the present as much as the past.

nary_nodes.label: Friedman criticizes democracy and urges action
evidence: Friedman criticized what he called a "bored, decadent democracy" and urged everyone present and everyone listening — as well as those outside the hall who remain "silent and grumbling"— to become active witnesses to their own time, before it is too late once again.

nary_nodes.label: Friedman's statement on Germany's community
evidence: "My country, Germany, is a community. This community is defined by diversity, and diversity has once again become a concept that is under heavy attack. Yet this community and this diversity are the only future we have," he said.

nary_nodes.label: Nike Wagner on "Wagner's artistic ritual"
evidence: Nike Wagner, the composer's great-granddaughter, summed up the message behind the work in her festival address: As visitors to the festival's grand hall, we become part of "Wagner's artistic ritual. Whoever takes a seat here now, sits with all those who have sat here before."

nary_nodes.label: Katharina Wagner on family's Nazi ties
evidence: Katharina Wagner, Richard Wagner's descendant and the festival's artistic director spoke candidly about her family's Nazi ties. "Given my family's close and, in some cases, deeply personal ties to the Nazi regime, and given the role of the festival as a cultural showcase of the Third Reich, but also bearing in mind that our German democracy today is once again threatened by forces seeking to make antisemitism, racism, chauvinism, and nationalism part of the foundations of the state, there is no better place than this Festspielhaus to say: No."

nary_nodes.label: Merz explains Wagner's legacy
evidence: In his speech, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz explained why, for him personally, Wagner's legacy and music represent the contradictions of German intellectual history: "Richard Wagner's person and work are exemplary of both the greatness and the darker depths of Germany's artistic and historical legacy. They represent the uniquely German combination of the most admirable and the most questionable aspects of our past. When we engage with Wagner, we have the opportunity to see and hear so much of ourselves across the centuries in a single body of work."
